items.name: Palacio Salvo
items.kicker: Art Deco tower over Plaza Independencia
items.body:
Completed in 1928 and briefly the tallest building in South America, this Art Deco landmark anchors Plaza Independencia. The only way inside is a guided tour (≈45 min) that reaches the 11th-floor terrace and rooftop viewpoint, plus a small tango museum honoring "La Cumparsita" composer Gerardo Matos Rodríguez, who lived here.

⚠ Red Ticket lists the tour a month at a time, as a new event page per month — which is why quoted time grids differ between sources, and why the February 2027 slots will not exist until close to the trip. Work from the Palacio Salvo producer page rather than any single dated listing.

items.name: Mercado del Puerto
items.kicker: 1868 iron-frame market hall turned parrilla hall
items.body:
A cast-iron Victorian market building inaugurated October 10, 1868, now packed wall-to-wall with parrilla counters grilling in the open, tourists and locals shoulder to shoulder at lunch. The building itself keeps Mon–Sat 9:00–17:00, Sun 10:00–17:00 hours, with exterior bars running later — Sunday is the busiest day, and 11:30–15:00 is the market's own recommended window for atmosphere and live music.

Treat it as a lunch stop. The hall's posted hours close at 17:00, and the later hours quoted for individual parrillas — El Palenque among them — are directory listings the restaurants don't publish themselves. El Palenque is closed Mondays; other stalls keep their own hours.

items.name: Museo del Carnaval
items.kicker: The story behind the world's longest Carnival
items.body: A small, well-organized museum on La Rambla near the port, tracing the history of Montevideo's Carnival — the candombe drum tradition, the Desfile de Llamadas parade, and the murga theatrical groups that compete every summer. A useful primer before the Carnival-holiday days on this trip.

items.name: Colonia del Sacramento — Barrio Histórico & Faro
items.body:
Twelve compact blocks of Portuguese and Spanish colonial streets, cobbled in uneven river stone, declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1995. Climb the 1857 lighthouse (built over the ruins of a burned convent) for the view over the old town and the Río de la Plata toward Argentina.

The old town itself is open every day. The lighthouse climb is Thursday–Sunday only, and ⚠ runs subject to Navy staff being on site, so it can be closed on the day. The quarter's indoor museums are the wet-weather answer — eight of them share one {{fact:colonia-museos-150-uyu}} ticket.

Day-tripper ferries from Buenos Aires land and depart roughly 10:00–15:00; the old town is noticeably quieter before or after that window, including into the evening once the crowds have left. Before 10:00 and after 15:00 is the Colonia del Sacramento off-peak visit window, when the old town reads as a quiet river settlement rather than a day-tripper stop.

items.name: Casapueblo — Punta Ballena
items.kicker: Carlos Páez Vilaró's cliffside whitewashed compound
items.body: Artist Carlos Páez Vilaró built this rambling, whitewashed, Gaudí-esque compound into the cliffs at Punta Ballena over four decades, living and working here until his death in 2014. Part gallery, part hotel, part sunset viewpoint — it's one of the few reliably-crowded sunset spots on this coast, for good reason.

items.name: La Mano de Punta del Este
items.kicker: The half-buried hand on Playa Brava
items.body: Chilean sculptor Mario Irarrázabal's 1982 concrete hand, fingers reaching out of the sand on Playa Brava — Punta del Este's single most photographed spot and free to visit any time. Early morning avoids the tour-bus crowds.

items.claim: Skip Uruguay's Carnival — Rio's is the famous one.
items.correction: Uruguay's is a different tradition, not a lesser version of Rio's: it runs longer than any other Carnival in the world (roughly 40 days, starting in January), and it's built on candombe drumming and the Llamadas parade — a distinct Afro-Uruguayan heritage, not a samba spectacle.

items.claim: Colonia del Sacramento is a Buenos Aires day trip, so see it from Argentina.
items.correction: It's just as reachable — and simpler — from Montevideo: a direct COT bus (≈2h20m, no international ferry crossing) runs from Tres Cruces terminal several times a day.

items.claim: Walk up to Palacio Salvo and buy a ticket at the door.
items.correction: There is no door sale — tours are booked exclusively through Red Ticket, and showing up without a ticket means no entry. Red Ticket posts them one month at a time, so book the February 2027 listing once it appears.
